pool.prompt: An 811 locate ticket returns yellow flags marking a gas line 3 feet south of a proposed bore path, with the bore passing within 18 inches of the gas main at closest approach. What is the correct next step before boring begins?
choices: Begin boring — 18 inches of separation from the locate mark is already code-compliant

Pothole-expose the gas main at the point of closest approach to confirm its actual depth and lateral position before boring — locate marks are approximate, and the actual gas main could be significantly closer than the flag indicates, putting the real separation well below any required minimum once boring is underway
Move the bore path to increase separation to at least 36 inches without exposing the utility
Call the gas company and ask them to relocate the gas main before proceeding
pool.explanation: Locate marks are approximate, not exact — typical locate tolerance can be off by a foot or more, meaning an 18-inch clearance from the flag could actually be a much smaller real-world separation. Standard practice (consistent with CGA Best Practices excavation-safety guidance) is to pothole-expose the utility at the closest-approach point and build the bore path from the CONFIRMED position, not the approximate locate mark.
pool.citation: CGA (Common Ground Alliance) Best Practices excavation-safety guidance — WebSearch-verified as an established industry excavation-safety reference (corroborated via bluestakes.org's CGA Best Practices Appendix B document).

pool.prompt: Orange flags are placed along the edge of a property during a residential 811 locate. What utility do orange flags mark, per the APWA Uniform Color Code?
choices: Electric power lines
Gas or oil lines
Telecommunications or CATV
Potable water
pool.explanation: Per the APWA Uniform Color Code: Red = electric power, Yellow = gas/oil/steam/petroleum, Orange = communication/alarm/signal lines (telecom/CATV), Blue = water/irrigation. The orange flags mark existing telecommunications infrastructure — likely a copper or fiber run belonging to an incumbent carrier, cable provider, or competitive fiber carrier.
pool.citation: APWA Uniform Color Code — WebSearch-verified (apwa.org official color code PDF, multiple independent corroborating 811/locate-industry sources).

pool.prompt: A crew plowing a residential route notices unidentified paint markings in the yard that don't appear on the 811 locate sheet. What should they do?
choices: Continue plowing — if it were important, it would already be on the locate sheet
Move the plow path 2 feet away from the marking and continue without further investigation

Stop work and manually investigate the marking (pothole-expose if needed) before resuming mechanized excavation — unidentified marks could be an expired prior locate, a private lateral not in the 811 system, or a survey mark, and any of these possibilities warrants confirming what's actually there before continuing
Report the discrepancy to the 811 center and continue mechanized excavation while waiting for a response
pool.explanation: Unidentified marks are exactly the kind of ambiguous field observation that requires stopping and investigating rather than assuming a benign explanation — moving the path by 2 feet doesn't resolve the ambiguity, since an unidentified utility could extend laterally beyond the mark in an unknown direction.

pool.prompt: A fiber conduit runs parallel to an electric supply conduit for 600 feet in a shared utility corridor. The electric is at 24-inch depth; the fiber is planned at 36-inch depth, 18 inches to the south (12 inches vertical separation, 18 inches horizontal separation — both exceeding typical code minimums). Is there any remaining concern?
choices: No — vertical and horizontal separation both exceeding typical minimums means the design is fully complete with no further action needed

The separation distances are likely code-compliant, but parallel runs in a shared utility corridor typically ALSO require coordination with the existing utility owner — the electric utility may require an encroachment permit, notification, or inspection for a 600-ft parallel run even when separation distances are met; 'code-compliant separation' and 'no coordination required' are not the same thing
Yes — fiber must always be installed north of electric supply lines to comply with NESC underground rules, regardless of actual separation distance
Yes — 18-inch horizontal separation is always non-compliant regardless of context
pool.explanation: Meeting the separation-distance minimum addresses only one dimension of a shared-corridor parallel run — the procedural/coordination requirement (permit, notification, inspection from the existing utility owner) is a separate consideration that a design satisfying only the distance minimum can still miss, which is why 'compliant separation' shouldn't be assumed to mean 'fully cleared for construction.'

pool.prompt: Match each APWA flag color to the utility it marks.
pool.explanation: The APWA Uniform Color Code standardizes utility-marking colors nationwide: Red for electric, Yellow for gas/oil/petroleum, Orange for telecom/CATV, and Blue for potable water — a fiber crew needs to recognize all four (plus Green/sewer and Purple/reclaimed water) to correctly interpret any 811 locate.
pool.citation: APWA Uniform Color Code — reused from T06-L06-Q2 verification.

pool.prompt: Why does the correct response to an unidentified utility marking (Q3) mirror the correct response to a marked gas line at closer-than-expected separation (Q1), even though one scenario involves a known utility and the other an unknown one?
choices: The two scenarios don't actually share a common principle; they require entirely different responses

Both scenarios share the same underlying principle: don't proceed with mechanized excavation based on an ASSUMED position or identity when the actual field evidence (a locate mark's approximate tolerance, or an unmarked flag) leaves genuine uncertainty — the correct response in both cases is to stop and physically confirm the actual condition (pothole-expose or manually investigate) before continuing
The gas-line scenario requires immediate evacuation, while the unidentified-marking scenario requires only a brief pause
Only the gas-line scenario is a genuine safety issue; the unidentified-marking scenario is purely a documentation concern
pool.explanation: Both scenarios reduce to the same underlying principle: field evidence with genuine uncertainty (approximate locate tolerance, or an unidentified mark) should never be resolved by assumption — the correct response is always to physically confirm the actual condition before mechanized excavation proceeds, regardless of whether the utility in question is a known, marked line or an unidentified marking.

pool.prompt: A designer assumes that meeting NESC-based separation minimums between a fiber conduit and a parallel electric supply line automatically satisfies every requirement for building in that shared corridor. What is the gap in this assumption?
choices: There is no gap; separation-distance compliance is the only requirement for any shared-corridor installation

Separation distance addresses the PHYSICAL clearance requirement, but shared-corridor construction often has a SEPARATE procedural requirement — coordination with the existing utility owner (permit, notification, inspection) — that isn't satisfied merely by meeting the distance minimum; a designer who only checks separation distance can still be missing a required coordination step
NESC separation minimums are only advisory and have no bearing on shared-corridor design at all
The gap only applies to gas lines, never to electric supply lines
pool.explanation: This is the Q4 principle stated generally: physical separation-distance compliance and procedural coordination requirements are two independent dimensions of shared-corridor construction, and satisfying one doesn't automatically satisfy the other — a complete design check verifies both.

pool.prompt: A field crew sees green flags along a route and, unsure what they mark, assumes they're a duplicate of the nearby orange (telecom) flags. What is the risk of this assumption, and what is the correct action instead?
choices: There is no risk; green and orange flags always mark the same utility category under the APWA color code

Green flags mark sewer/drain lines — a completely different utility category from orange (telecom/CATV); assuming they're duplicative rather than confirming the actual APWA color-code meaning risks missing a real sewer-line hazard during excavation. The correct action is to confirm the actual meaning of each flag color present (per the APWA code) rather than assuming any two colors are interchangeable
Green flags are purely decorative and don't correspond to any utility
The risk only matters if the crew is using open-cut trenching, not for HDD or plowing
pool.explanation: Green flags mark an entirely distinct utility category (sewer/drain) from orange (telecom/CATV) under the APWA color code — treating any two flag colors as interchangeable without confirming their actual meaning risks missing a genuinely different utility hazard, reinforcing that a crew needs to know the full color code, not just the colors relevant to their own utility type.
